column5: basis
Git's origin as a distributed VCS and why companies still need a centralized host.
Packfiles as Git's storage and network unit; why one server with an on-disk repository has a low ceiling.
Three ways to distribute Git; object-level distribution in a DHT via JGit at Google, dropped because clone needs packfiles and DAG walks need round trips.
Early GitHub keeps the Rails app unchanged and tries to distribute the filesystem; NFS discarded as slow and buggy.
Block-level replication (GFS, DRBD) hard to operate; scattered packfile layout defeats networked filesystems; move to RPC fileservers with a single copy per repository.
Spokes's three choices: packfile level, plain repositories on local NVMe, replicas kept consistently in sync; Git clients need strong consistency.
Spokes fans out packfiles then runs three-phase commit on the reference transaction; reads served by any replica.
Three-phase commit tail latency limits replica count for monorepos, and the three-replica floor is wasteful for many small agent repositories.
Disk replicas as source of truth make repositories pets: routing database, checksums, fast repair, quorum loss on two corrupt copies.
Continuity stores each push as a WAL entry in S3, publishes via a local reference transaction and WAL index, batches writes; keeps Spokes's plain NVMe repositories.
Repositories as a warm cache rematerialized from the WAL; rendezvous hashing instead of routing tables; any node can be primary thanks to CAS on S3; contrasted with Spokes.
Optimistic UDP gossip replication with conditional GETs against S3; any number of replicas, from hundreds for monorepos to zero for idle repositories.
Compaction needed for both WAL and packfiles; Spokes repacks on every replica with failover risk, Continuity compacts on the primary and replicas download the result.
Replication and compaction drive behaviour under load; linear read scaling to 100 replicas; push throughput bound by S3 write latency and compaction speed.
Azure DevOps stores packfiles in blob storage and references in SQL Server; Continuity avoids the external database, keeping the WAL as provenance and the single source of truth.
Origin as Cursor's production platform; agents raise the stakes of Git hosting reliability.
Spokes replicates at the Git application level through a proxy; early versions needed nearby replicas, motivating geo-distribution.
DRBD block replication before Spokes forced adjacent replicas; distant replicas limit the reference-update rate, which bookkeeping updates make critical.
Three-phase commit costs four round trips to distant replicas, also serving as a distributed lock; overlapping work with network waits.
Transactional reference updates added to upstream Git so replicas can prepare and commit or roll back deterministically; faster reference updates.
Incremental XOR checksum over references summarizes and compares replica state after every update.
Coalescing and deprioritizing bookkeeping updates; reads routed to the nearest in-sync replica; non-voting geo-replicas in GitHub Enterprise.
Spokes (formerly DGit) keeps at least three copies of every repository, replicating, repairing and rebalancing with Git and rsync.
Availability vs durability and CAP; Spokes prioritizes consistency and partition tolerance, refusing writes it cannot commit to two replicas.
Failure detection from real application traffic rather than heartbeats alone; node marked offline after three failed requests.
Routing returns a preference-ordered list of replicas for failover; offline marking is advisory; M-by-N failure detection per application server.
Incident shows per-application-server detection containing a fault; replicas in different racks, writes require a strict majority with locks that serialize concurrent writes.
Majority sizing for three to five replicas; every write is its own vote instead of a fixed primary; losing replicas are marked unhealthy and repaired N-to-N.
Planned reboots quiesce a server so long-running reads such as clones finish while writes keep flowing.
Rolling rack-by-rack reboots instead of chaos testing; unplugging a server leaves repositories at two copies and raises write-rejection risk.
Retire servers by removing them from the active replica count so repairs run first; summary of three replicas, majority writes, traffic-based failure detection and automated repair.
Scalar configures upstream Git features rather than adding its own; GVFS protocol is the one non-upstream part, an older form of partial clone.
What scalar register and scalar clone enable: index compression, background fetch and maintenance, filesystem monitor, partial clone, sparse-checkout, src layout.
VFS for Git virtualizes the filesystem for the Windows repository; Scalar supports very large repositories without virtualization via config and background maintenance.
Scalar works with any host; registering a repository sets config and starts background maintenance with logs.
Foreground maintenance with scalar run; cloning with the GVFS protocol from Azure Repos needs co-located cache servers, otherwise use the plain Git protocol.
scalar clone gives a sparse cone-mode working directory under src so build outputs sit outside the repository.
Core commands scale with index, populated and modified size; the index format is compressed for the Windows repository.
Sparse-checkout reduces the populated size; scalar clone is sparse by default.
Filesystem monitor with Watchman limits scanning to modified paths; git status timings for Office.
GVFS protocol downloads only commits and trees and fetches objects on demand through co-located cache servers, coupling clients to a central server; inspired partial clone.
Expensive maintenance moved from foreground auto-GC to incremental background work, as in VFS for Git and Scalar.
Recommended config: auto-GC off, commit-graph written in the background, ahead/behind disabled, filesystem monitor hook.
Hourly background fetch into a hidden ref namespace and incremental commit-graph writes.
Loose-object cleanup and the multi-pack-index keep object lookup fast without a full repack.
Incremental repack of small packfiles via the multi-pack-index in two steps; pack counts and sizes drop for Windows repositories.
Scalar intends to do less as Git does more.
Planned upstream Git work: filesystem watcher, sparse-checkout, faster checkout without virtualization, partial clone with GVFS, cache-server-like fetch URLs, background maintenance.
Agents create both huge monorepos and many short-lived repositories; a fixed three-replica design fits neither.
Packfile layout unrelated to the commit DAG makes networked hops expensive; all approaches differ in where the real copy lives.
WAL in S3 as source of truth, local repositories as warm cache, rendezvous hashing; gives up consensus latency for S3 write latency.
Storing Git objects in a DHT via JGit; abandoned because graph traversal and packfile-based clone were too slow.
NFS, GFS and DRBD under an unchanged Git and Rails; abandoned because Git needs local-disk semantics.
Spokes replicates plain repositories with three-phase commit on reference transactions; later geo-replication improvements.
GVFS protocol with on-demand objects and cache servers, then Scalar using upstream partial clone, sparse-checkout and background maintenance.
Primary-only compaction downloaded by replicas trades bandwidth for CPU; compaction becomes the throughput limit.
Spokes needs three replicas per repository for correctness; Continuity makes replica count elastic, down to zero.
Consensus latency is bound by the slowest replica, so more replicas hurt writes; Continuity removes consensus at the cost of S3 latency.
Blob storage for Git data plus a relational database for references; rejected by Cursor as a second source of truth to keep consistent.
Side-by-side summary of five approaches, each intervening at a different layer.
Tracked disk replicas need routing metadata, checksums and fast repair; operational toil grows with repository count.
Git clients and automation cannot tolerate eventual consistency; reason Continuity acknowledges pushes only once durable.
Shift from quorum agreement as source of truth to an immutable log with replicas as caches.
Chronology from Git's design through filesystem distribution, the DHT, Spokes, GVFS and Scalar, to Continuity and Origin.
